title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Every website with a newsletter faces the same quiet dilemma: what do you actually say to get someone to sign up? The words you choose — your “call to action,” or CTA — can have a surprisingly large effect on whether a visitor clicks or scrolls past.
On our homepage, visitors can subscribe to our newsletter. We have two candidate CTAs we want to compare:

CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!”
CTA B: “Stay up to date — join our newsletter!”

Rather than guessing which one works better, we ran an A/B test. In an A/B test, incoming visitors are randomly assigned — like a coin flip — to see either CTA A or CTA B. We then compare the sign-up rates between the two groups. Randomization is the key ingredient: because assignment is random, any difference in sign-up rates is attributable to the CTA, not to differences in who happened to visit on which day.
This post walks through the statistical machinery behind that analysis — hypothesis testing, the Central Limit Theorem, bootstrap standard errors, and some common pitfalls — using simulation so we can see these ideas in action.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up or doesn’t — a binary outcome. We model each visitor’s outcome as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution: with probability \(\pi\), the visitor signs up (outcome = 1); otherwise they don’t (outcome = 0).
Because the CTA a visitor sees may influence their decision, we allow the sign-up probability to differ between groups:

Visitors seeing CTA A sign up with probability \(\pi_A\)
Visitors seeing CTA B sign up with probability \(\pi_B\)

The quantity we care about is the difference in sign-up rates:
\[\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B\]
If \(\theta > 0\), CTA A is better. If \(\theta < 0\), CTA B wins. If \(\theta = 0\), it doesn’t matter which we use.
We estimate \(\theta\) with the difference in sample proportions:
\[\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B = \hat\pi_A - \hat\pi_B\]
where \(\bar{X}_A\) is just the fraction of CTA A visitors who signed up (and similarly for B). Since each observation is 0 or 1, the sample mean equals the sample proportion. This estimator is intuitive, easy to compute, and has very nice statistical properties — as we’ll see.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real experiment, we wouldn’t know the true values of \(\pi_A\) and \(\pi_B\). But for the purpose of this walkthrough, we get to play the role of the universe: we’ll set the true parameters ourselves, run the test, and then check whether our statistical tools recover the truth we planted.
We set:

\(\pi_A = 0.22\) — 22% of visitors seeing CTA A sign up
\(\pi_B = 0.18\) — 18% of visitors seeing CTA B sign up
True difference: \(\theta = 0.04\)

We simulate 1,000 visitors per group (2,000 total):

np.random.seed(42)
pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n = 1000

group_A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
group_B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_hat = group_A.mean() - group_B.mean()
print(f"Observed difference (theta_hat): {theta_hat:.4f}")

Observed difference (theta_hat): 0.0380


Our observed difference is close to the true value of 0.04 — a promising sign. But how close is close enough, and how confident should we be? That’s what the rest of this post addresses.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers (LLN) states that as your sample size grows, the sample mean converges to the true population mean. For our estimator, this means \(\hat\theta = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B\) will get closer and closer to the true \(\theta = 0.04\) as we collect more data. The LLN is the foundation of why the A/B test works at all — it guarantees we can learn the truth if we’re patient enough.
We can watch this convergence happen in real time. For each of our 1,000 simulated pairs of observations, we compute the running (cumulative) average of the pairwise differences:

diffs = group_A - group_B
cumulative_avg = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)










With only a handful of observations, the estimate bounces wildly — it briefly suggests CTA B is much better, then overestimates CTA A’s advantage. But as the sample grows, the noise cancels out and the running average settles close to the true difference of 0.04 (the red dashed line). By around 400 observations, the estimate has largely stabilized.
This is the LLN at work: more data doesn’t just give you a better estimate, it guarantees convergence to the truth. It’s also a reminder that small samples can mislead — an analyst who stopped at 50 observations might have drawn a very wrong conclusion.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
Knowing our estimate will converge to the truth is reassuring, but it leaves open an important question: how precise is our estimate with the data we actually have? A single number like \(\hat\theta = 0.04\) is a point estimate — our best guess, but it doesn’t communicate uncertainty. For that, we need a confidence interval.
One elegant way to quantify uncertainty is the bootstrap. The idea is simple: since we can’t re-run the experiment thousands of times in reality, we simulate re-running it by resampling from our own data. Specifically:

Draw a new sample of size 1,000 with replacement from our observed CTA A data.
Do the same for CTA B.
Compute \(\hat\theta^* = \bar{X}_A^* - \bar{X}_B^*\) on these resamples.
Repeat 1,000 times. The standard deviation of those \(\hat\theta^*\) values is our bootstrap standard error.


B = 1000
boot_estimates = np.array([
    np.random.choice(group_A, size=n, replace=True).mean() -
    np.random.choice(group_B, size=n, replace=True).mean()
    for _ in range(B)
])

boot_se = boot_estimates.std()

pi_hat_A = group_A.mean()
pi_hat_B = group_B.mean()
analytical_se = np.sqrt(
    pi_hat_A * (1 - pi_hat_A) / n +
    pi_hat_B * (1 - pi_hat_B) / n
)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se

print(f"Bootstrap SE:   {boot_se:.5f}")
print(f"Analytical SE:  {analytical_se:.5f}")
print(f"95% CI:         [{ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f}]")

Using the bootstrap standard error, our 95% confidence interval for \(\theta\) is approximately \([`{ci_lower:.4f}`,\ `{ci_upper:.4f}`]\). Since this interval doesn’t contain zero, we have evidence that CTA A outperforms CTA B.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The confidence interval above relied on a crucial fact: for large samples, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately normally distributed — even though the underlying data are Bernoulli (just 0s and 1s, which couldn’t look less normal). This result is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), arguably the most important theorem in applied statistics.
The CLT says: regardless of the shape of the underlying distribution, the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately Normal as \(n\) grows. Since \(\hat\theta\) is a difference of two sample means, it inherits this property.
To see this visually, we repeat our experiment 1,000 times at four different sample sizes — \(n \in \{25, 50, 100, 500\}\) — and plot the distribution of \(\hat\theta\) each time:

def simulate_theta_hat(n_sim, reps=1000):
    return np.array([
        np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n_sim).mean() -
        np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n_sim).mean()
        for _ in range(reps)
    ])

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
clt_results = {n_val: simulate_theta_hat(n_val) for n_val in sample_sizes}










At \(n = 25\), the histogram is jagged and irregular — the Bernoulli origins of the data are still visible. By \(n = 100\), a bell shape is clearly emerging, centered on the true value of 0.04. At \(n = 500\), the distribution is smooth, tightly concentrated, and convincingly normal.
This is the CLT in action. It’s what allows us to use Normal-distribution-based tools (z-scores, confidence intervals, p-values) on data that are fundamentally binary. Notice also that the distributions get narrower as \(n\) grows — larger samples give more precise estimates, consistent with what the Law of Large Numbers told us earlier.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now we’re ready for a formal hypothesis test. The goal is to assess whether our data provide enough evidence to conclude that the two CTAs actually differ in effectiveness — or whether the observed \(\hat\theta\) could plausibly have arisen by chance even if the CTAs were identical.
We frame this as two competing hypotheses:

Null hypothesis \(H_0: \theta = 0\) — the CTAs perform equally; any observed difference is noise.
Alternative hypothesis \(H_1: \theta \neq 0\) — the CTAs differ in sign-up rates.

We compute a test statistic that tells us how many standard errors our estimate is away from zero:
\[z = \frac{\hat\theta - 0}{SE(\hat\theta)}\]
By the CLT, \(\hat\theta\) is approximately Normal for large samples. Under \(H_0\) (where the true mean is 0), dividing by its standard deviation gives a standard Normal distribution: \(z \;\dot\sim\; N(0, 1)\). This lets us compute a p-value: the probability of observing a \(|z|\) this large or larger if \(H_0\) were true.

Why do people call this a “t-test”? The classical t-test assumes the underlying data are Normal and the variance is unknown — producing an exact t-distribution. Our data are Bernoulli, not Normal, so there’s no exact t-distribution result here. The CLT gives us approximate Normality, and since we estimate the SE from data, we’re technically running a z-test. In practice, for large samples the t- and z-distributions are nearly identical — but it’s worth knowing why.


se_hat = analytical_se
z_stat = theta_hat / se_hat
p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))

print(f"Point estimate:  {theta_hat:.4f}")
print(f"Standard error:  {se_hat:.5f}")
print(f"Z-statistic:     {z_stat:.3f}")
print(f"P-value:         {p_value:.4f}")

With a z-statistic well above 1.96 and a p-value below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The data provide strong evidence that CTA A produces a higher sign-up rate than CTA B. Of course, in this simulation we know the truth — the test is correctly identifying the 0.04 difference we planted.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
Here’s a satisfying insight: the two-sample test we just ran is mathematically equivalent to a simple linear regression. Understanding this connection unlocks a much more flexible toolkit.
The setup: stack all 2,000 observations into a single dataset with two columns — \(Y_i\) (the outcome: 1 if signed up, 0 if not) and \(D_i\) (a group indicator: 1 for CTA A, 0 for CTA B). Then fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]
The coefficients have a clean interpretation:

When \(D_i = 0\) (CTA B): \(E[Y_i] = \beta_0\), so \(\hat\beta_0 = \hat\pi_B\)
When \(D_i = 1\) (CTA A): \(E[Y_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1\), so \(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 = \hat\pi_A\)
Therefore: \(\hat\beta_1 = \hat\pi_A - \hat\pi_B = \hat\theta\)

The OLS coefficient on the group indicator is numerically identical to our difference-in-means estimator.

D = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
X = sm.add_constant(D)

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
Imagine your boss is impatient. Instead of waiting for all 1,000 visitors per group, she wants to check the results every 100 visitors. If any of those 10 interim tests hits \(p < 0.05\), she wants to declare a winner and stop.
This practice — commonly called peeking — is one of the most widespread mistakes in A/B testing. A single test at \(\alpha = 0.05\) has a 5% false positive rate. But each peek is another independent chance to get lucky in the wrong direction. Across 10 peeks, the cumulative probability of at least one false positive climbs well above 5%.
Let’s demonstrate this. We set up a world where there is no true difference (\(\pi_A = \pi_B = 0.20\), so \(\theta = 0\)), then simulate 10,000 experiments:

np.random.seed(123)
n_experiments = 10000
peek_points = np.arange(100, 1001, 100)

false_positive_peek = np.zeros(n_experiments, dtype=bool)
false_positive_single = np.zeros(n_experiments, dtype=bool)

for i in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, 1000)

    for k in peek_points:
        pA = A_null[:k].mean()
        pB = B_null[:k].mean()
        se_k = np.sqrt(pA*(1-pA)/k + pB*(1-pB)/k)
        if se_k == 0:
            continue
        if 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs((pA - pB) / se_k))) < 0.05:
            false_positive_peek[i] = True
            break

    pA_f, pB_f = A_null.mean(), B_null.mean()
    se_f = np.sqrt(pA_f*(1-pA_f)/1000 + pB_f*(1-pB_f)/1000)
    if se_f > 0:
        false_positive_single[i] = (
            2*(1-stats.norm.cdf(abs((pA_f-pB_f)/se_f))) < 0.05
        )

fp_peek_rate = false_positive_peek.mean()
fp_single_rate = false_positive_single.mean()

print(f"Single-test FP rate: {fp_single_rate:.3f}")
print(f"Peeking FP rate:     {fp_peek_rate:.3f}")

Single-test FP rate: 0.052
Peeking FP rate:     0.199










The Cost of Peeking

A single end-of-experiment test produces a false positive rate right around the promised 5%. But peeking 10 times inflates it to around {fp_peek_rate:.0%} — roughly three times the nominal level.
In practice, this means a company running A/B tests with peeking will regularly declare winners that don’t exist. The fix? Commit to your sample size before running the experiment and test exactly once at the end. If early stopping is genuinely necessary, use methods designed for it — like sequential testing or the Bonferroni correction — which account for multiple looks explicitly.

This post was written as an exploration of classical frequentist statistics through simulation. All data are synthetic.

title: Replication of Karlan and List (2007)
text:
Karlan and List (2007) conducted one of the most influential natural field experiments in the economics of charitable giving. The authors partnered with a liberal US nonprofit organization to send direct mail solicitations to over 50,000 prior donors. The central question is whether price — as manipulated through matching grants — affects both the likelihood and amount of charitable giving.
The experimental design randomly assigned donors to a control group (no match offer) or one of several treatment groups varying along three dimensions: (1) the match ratio ($1:$1, $2:$1, or $3:$1), (2) the maximum size of the matching grant ($25,000, $50,000, $100,000, or unstated), and (3) the suggested donation amount (equal to, 1.25×, or 1.5× the donor’s highest previous contribution).
The paper’s headline findings are:

Simply announcing a matching grant increases response rates by ~22% and revenue per solicitation by ~19%.
Contrary to conventional fundraising wisdom, larger match ratios (2:1, 3:1) have no additional effect over a 1:1 match.
Treatment effects are heterogeneous by political environment: the match worked strongly in “red” states but had little effect in “blue” states.

These findings challenge the common fundraising belief that bigger matches attract bigger responses, and raise interesting questions about the role of political identity in charitable behavior.

text:
Conclusion
This replication confirms all three main findings of Karlan and List (2007):

Matching grants work — announcing a match significantly increases participation and revenue.
Match ratio doesn’t matter — 2:1 and 3:1 perform identically to 1:1, refuting conventional fundraising wisdom.
Context matters enormously — the entire effect is driven by red-state donors, pointing to non-price factors like political identity.

Causal inference is valid here because of random assignment: the balance table confirms groups were equivalent on all pre-treatment observables, so any difference in outcomes is attributable to the match offer itself — not to who received it.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Blueprinty is a small software company that sells tools for engineering firms developing blueprint documentation specifically for US patent applications. Their marketing team wants to argue that firms using Blueprinty’s software are more successful at getting patents approved — a potentially powerful selling point, but one that requires careful empirical backing.
To investigate the claim, Blueprinty collected data on 1,500 mature (non-startup) engineering firms, capturing each firm’s number of patents awarded over the last five years, its regional location, years since incorporation, and whether it currently uses Blueprinty’s software.
While this dataset is useful, evaluating the marketing claim is not straightforward. Blueprinty’s customers self-selected into using the product — they were not randomly assigned to it. As a result, simple comparisons between customers and non-customers may be misleading: if, for instance, older and more established firms are both more likely to adopt Blueprinty’s software and more likely to receive patents, then we might observe a positive correlation between software usage and patent counts that has nothing to do with the software itself. Properly evaluating the claim requires a modeling approach that accounts for these pre-existing differences across firms.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
Patent counts are non-negative integers — exactly the type of outcome for which the Normal distribution is a poor fit. A Normal model would assign positive probability to negative values and non-integer values, neither of which can occur. The Poisson distribution is the natural starting point for non-negative integer count outcomes. It is characterized by a single parameter \(\lambda > 0\), which equals both the mean and the variance of the distribution.

Likelihood and Log-Likelihood
For a single observation \(Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), the probability mass function is:
\[f(Y_i \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}\]
Assuming the \(n = 1{,}500\) observations are independent and identically distributed, the joint likelihood is the product of the individual pmfs:
\[L(\lambda \mid \mathbf{Y}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\,\lambda^{Y_i}}{Y_i!}\]
Taking the natural log converts the product into a sum and makes optimization tractable:
\[\ell(\lambda \mid \mathbf{Y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[-\lambda + Y_i\ln\lambda - \ln(Y_i!)\right] = -n\lambda + \left(\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)\ln\lambda - \sum_{i=1}^n \ln(Y_i!)\]


Analytic MLE
Differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to \(\lambda\) and setting equal to zero:
\[\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda} = -n + \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i}{\lambda} = 0 \implies \hat\lambda_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i = \bar{Y}\]
This is reassuring: the MLE is simply the sample mean, which makes intuitive sense because \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \lambda\) for a Poisson random variable.


Log-Likelihood Function and Plot


Code
Y = df["patents"].values

def poisson_loglik(lam, Y):
    """Log-likelihood of Poisson(lambda) for observed counts Y."""
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * np.log(lam) - gammaln(Y + 1))

# Plot over a range of lambda values
lambdas  = np.linspace(0.5, 8, 500)
log_liks = [poisson_loglik(l, Y) for l in lambdas]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(lambdas, log_liks, color="#2563EB", linewidth=2.5)
ax.axvline(Y.mean(), color="#EF4444", linestyle="--", linewidth=2,
           label=f"$\\hat{{\\lambda}}_{{\\mathrm{{MLE}}}} = \\bar{{Y}} = {Y.mean():.4f}$")
ax.set_xlabel("$\\lambda$", fontsize=13)
ax.set_ylabel("Log-Likelihood $\\ell(\\lambda)$", fontsize=12)

The log-likelihood curve is unimodal and concave, peaking at \(\lambda \approx 3.68\) — the sample mean. Reading the MLE off the plot is straightforward: it is the value of \(\lambda\) at which the curve reaches its maximum. The red dashed line confirms this visually.


Numerical Maximization

The numerical optimizer recovers essentially the same value as the closed-form solution. The tiny rounding difference (on the order of \(10^{-8}\)) arises from the stopping tolerance of the optimizer, not from any mathematical discrepancy — confirming that the log-likelihood surface has a single peak exactly at \(\bar{Y}\).

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Poisson Regression
The simple Poisson model treats all firms as identical, which we know is incorrect — firms differ in age, region, and software usage. We now extend the model by allowing each firm’s rate parameter to vary with its observed characteristics:
\[Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i) \qquad \text{where} \qquad \lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\]
Here \(X_i\) is a row vector of covariates for firm \(i\) and \(\beta\) is a vector of coefficients to be estimated. We use the exponential link \(\lambda_i = \exp(X_i'\beta)\) for a fundamental reason: \(\lambda_i\) must be strictly positive, yet \(X_i'\beta\) is an unconstrained real number. The exponential function maps the real line onto the positive reals, ensuring predictions are always valid.

Log-Likelihood for Poisson Regression


Code
# ── Build the design matrix ──────────────────────────────────────────────
region_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["region"], drop_first=False).drop(columns=["Northeast"])
age   = df["age"].values
age2  = age ** 2
iscust = df["iscustomer"].values
n = len(Y)

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), age, age2, region_dummies.values, iscust])
col_names = (["intercept", "age", "age_sq"]
             + region_dummies.columns.tolist()
             + ["iscustomer"])

print("Design matrix shape:", X.shape)
print("Columns:", col_names)

Columns: ['intercept', 'age', 'age_sq', 'Midwest', 'Northwest', 'South', 'Southwest', 'iscustomer']


The design matrix includes:

Intercept: the baseline log-rate.
Age and Age²: a quadratic in firm age, because the relationship between firm maturity and patenting activity is unlikely to be perfectly linear — young firms may be building capacity, mature firms at their peak, and very old firms slowing down.
Regional indicators for Midwest, Northwest, South, and Southwest, with Northeast as the reference category. One region must be omitted to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept (the dummy variable trap).
iscustomer: the binary variable of primary interest.



Code
def poisson_reg_loglik(beta, Y, X):
    """Log-likelihood of Poisson regression."""
    Xb  = np.clip(X @ beta, -500, 500)
    lam = np.exp(Xb)
    return np.sum(-lam + Y * Xb - gammaln(Y + 1))

def neg_reg_loglik(beta):
    return -poisson_reg_loglik(beta, Y, X)

def grad_neg(beta):
    Xb  = np.clip(X @ beta, -500, 500)
    lam = np.exp(Xb)
    return X.T @ (lam - Y)




Finding the MLE Numerically


Code
result_reg = optimize.minimize(
    neg_reg_loglik,
    np.zeros(len(col_names)),
    method="L-BFGS-B",
    jac=grad_neg,
    options={"maxiter": 50_000, "ftol": 1e-15, "gtol": 1e-8},
)
beta_hat = result_reg.x
print("Optimizer converged:", result_reg.success)

# ── Numerical Hessian for standard errors ────────────────────────────────
p   = len(beta_hat)
eps = 1e-5
H   = np.zeros((p, p))
for i in range(p):
    for j in range(p):
        ei = np.zeros(p); ei[i] = eps
        ej = np.zeros(p); ej[j] = eps
        H[i, j] = (neg_reg_loglik(beta_hat+ei+ej)
                   - neg_reg_loglik(beta_hat+ei-ej)
                   - neg_reg_loglik(beta_hat-ei+ej)
                   + neg_reg_loglik(beta_hat-ei-ej)) / (4*eps*eps)

se_optim = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(H)))


Optimizer converged: True


Standard errors come from the observed Fisher information: the negative inverse Hessian of the log-likelihood evaluated at the MLE. Intuitively, a very curved (tight) log-likelihood means the data are informative and the MLE is precise; a flat log-likelihood means the MLE is uncertain. The square roots of the diagonal elements of \((-H)^{-1}\) are the asymptotic standard errors.

The standard errors are also very close; any small discrepancies reflect the finite-difference approximation used in our numerical Hessian versus the analytic information matrix that statsmodels computes internally. This cross-check validates our implementation.


Interpreting the Coefficients









The results make substantive sense:

Age (positive) and Age² (negative) together describe an inverted-U relationship: patent output first rises as firms mature and build R&D capacity, then tapers off among the oldest firms. Both effects are precisely estimated.
Regional indicators are small and statistically indistinguishable from zero, suggesting that after accounting for age and customer status, region adds little predictive power.
iscustomer (0.208, SE 0.031) is the coefficient of primary interest. It is positive, statistically significant, and implies that using Blueprinty’s software is associated with roughly \(e^{0.208} - 1 \approx 23\%\) more expected patents, holding all else constant. The coefficient is highlighted in red in the chart above.

title: Poisson Regression and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Effect of Blueprinty’s Software
Poisson regression coefficients operate on the multiplicative scale of \(\lambda\), so \(\hat\beta_{\text{iscustomer}} = 0.208\) means the expected patent rate is multiplied by \(e^{0.208} \approx 1.23\) for customers. To translate this into a more concrete, additive quantity — extra patents per firm — we use the counterfactual prediction approach.


Code
# Counterfactual datasets
X0 = X.copy(); X0[:, -1] = 0   # set every firm to non-customer
X1 = X.copy(); X1[:, -1] = 1   # set every firm to customer

y_hat_0 = np.exp(np.clip(X0 @ beta_hat, -500, 500))
y_hat_1 = np.exp(np.clip(X1 @ beta_hat, -500, 500))

avg_effect = np.mean(y_hat_1 - y_hat_0)
print(f"Average predicted patents (non-customer):  {y_hat_0.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Average predicted patents (customer):      {y_hat_1.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Average treatment effect (ATE):            {avg_effect:.3f}")


Average predicted patents (non-customer):  3.436
Average predicted patents (customer):      4.229
Average treatment effect (ATE):            0.793











Holding each firm’s age and region fixed at its observed values, switching every firm from non-customer to customer status is predicted to increase patent awards by an average of 0.79 patents over five years — roughly one additional patent every six years per firm. The distribution is right-skewed because the multiplicative effect is larger in absolute terms for older, more prolific firms.

Conclusion
The Poisson regression analysis provides evidence consistent with Blueprinty’s marketing claim: after controlling for firm age and regional location, customers are associated with materially higher patent approval rates. The estimated average treatment effect is approximately +0.79 patents per firm over five years.
That said, two important caveats apply. First, this is an observational study: firms chose whether to adopt Blueprinty’s software, so unobserved characteristics (e.g., internal R&D investment, team quality, strategic focus on patentable innovations) could drive both software adoption and patent success simultaneously. Without random assignment, we cannot rule out residual confounding. Second, the Poisson model assumes that the conditional mean equals the conditional variance; if patent counts exhibit overdispersion in practice, a negative binomial model would be more appropriate. Despite these caveats, the magnitude and statistical significance of the customer effect are sufficiently robust to warrant continued investigation — and to provide preliminary support for the marketing team’s position.

title: Design System
text:
Visual foundations and component inventory. This doc mirrors the CSS — if it disagrees with styles/custom.css, the CSS wins. Keep this in sync when you change tokens, add components, or alter the theming model.




Zero Bootstrap, zero Quarto defaults. theme: none + minimal: true in _quarto.yml. Every pixel is authored.
Dark-first, light as a refined variant. Dark mode is the default (set pre-paint in _partials/head-extras.html via inline <script>); light mode adds targeted overrides in a single html:not(.dark) block at the end of the CSS.
Liquid glass aesthetic on .navbar, .badge, .theme-pill, .cell:not(.terminal-cell), .copy-btn, .btn-primary (dark). Terminal is explicitly opaque — it represents a code environment, not a UI panel.
Gradient = identity. Blue→violet (#3B82F6 → #A78BFA) appears in accents, hover shadows, splash buttons, project card glow. Layered box-shadow fakes gradient borders without border-image (which conflicts with border-radius).
Zero JS dependencies. Vanilla fetch() for JSON data, vanilla mousemove listeners for the cursor effects.





Defined at the top of styles/custom.css. All color edits happen here and nowhere else.

--bg-sec:         #161614   /* secondary / striped bg */

Pre-paint default: _partials/head-extras.html contains <script>document.documentElement.classList.add('dark');</script> — runs before any CSS applies, prevents flash of light mode.
Toggle: js/main.js section 1 toggles html.dark on click; swaps #theme-icon (sun/moon SVG) and #theme-label (“Dark”/“Light”). No localStorage persistence currently.
Scoping:

Dark styles use html.dark prefix (or are unprefixed because dark is the default).
Light-mode corrections live in a dedicated html:not(.dark) block at the end of the CSS (see decision 11). This block handles contrast fixes, card separation, glass effects, blob re-coloring.

What’s not themed: The terminal cell (.terminal-cell — always #0D0D0C), the pulsing availability dot color (#4ADE80).





Three layered effects driven by js/main.js sections 5–6. Touch devices (hover: none) are fully excluded from the grid/spotlight effect.

Blob parallax (--blob-x, --blob-y) — .hero-inner::after follows cursor at 35% strength, LERP 0.09, MAX_DRIFT=120px, returns to origin after 3s idle. Global mousemove listener so the blob responds anywhere on the page, not just over the hero.
Grid parallax (--grid-x, --grid-y) — very slow LERP (0.035), MAX_SHIFT=4px — subtle drift of the dot pattern.
Spotlight (--mouse-x, --mouse-y) — direct cursor tracking, no lerp (any delay reads as lag). Sets radial gradient at cursor position, lighting nearby dots. Hides to -500px off-screen on mouseleave.

On non-homepage pages, the same system attaches to document.body for an ambient version (reduced opacity).




Single breakpoint at @media (max-width: 768px) at the end of styles/custom.css. Mobile collapses multi-column grids to 1 column, reduces padding from 64px → 24px, and hides .nav-links (no hamburger — site targets desktop recruiters primarily).




Append or edit here when you: - Add, rename, or remove a color token - Change the font family or typography scale - Add a new component class that isn’t a one-off - Change the theming mechanism (e.g. add localStorage persistence, add a third mode) - Change the cursor-effect system (new interactions, new parallax layers)
For one-off tweaks to an existing component (hover color, padding adjustment), do not update this doc — the CSS is the source of truth and this doc only covers structure.

title: marketing analytics
section: The measurement was correct. The model was broken.
text:
The measurement was correct. The model was broken.
Every metric embeds a theory — an implicit claim about what the number means. DAU is a proxy for engagement. Engagement is a proxy for value delivered. Value delivered is a proxy for willingness to pay. Willingness to pay is a proxy for revenue.
When DAU went up, the team assumed the whole chain held. It didn’t. Users were active but not finding value. They were clicking around, confused. Confusion generates activity. Activity looks like engagement. Engagement looks like growth.
The metric was accurate. The theory behind it was wrong.

title: marketing analytics
text:
We mistake precision for validity
A thermometer can tell you the temperature in a room to two decimal places. That doesn’t tell you if the room is comfortable for a human being. We’ve built a data culture that is obsessed with precision but careless about validity.
Precision is a property of measurement. Validity is a property of the relationship between the measurement and what you actually care about. You can have one without the other. Most dashboards optimize for precision and assume validity.

title: marketing analytics
text:
The question that fixes it
Before you build any metric, ask: what decision does this change?
If DAU goes up by 10%, what do you do differently? If the answer is “we celebrate and keep doing what we’re doing,” the metric isn’t driving decisions — it’s decorating them. You’re not measuring to learn. You’re measuring to confirm.
The useful metrics are the ones that make you act asymmetrically. High number → one action. Low number → different action. If both outcomes lead to the same plan, the metric is noise dressed as signal.

title: marketing analytics
text:
Dashboards are not understanding
A dashboard shows you what happened. It says nothing about why. And it is completely silent on what to do next.
Understanding requires a model — a causal story about the world. Dashboards show you symptoms. Models explain mechanisms. Most teams invest heavily in dashboards and lightly in models, then wonder why they keep being surprised.
The dashboard that lied wasn’t broken. The team’s mental model of what it meant was.

Measurement is a tool for thinking, not a substitute for it.

title: marketing analytics
section: The Problem Disguised as a Button
text:
The Problem Disguised as a Button
Let’s say you have two calls to action on your landing page.
CTA A: “Sign up for our newsletter here!” CTA B: “Stay up to date by signing up!”
They’re nearly identical. But you suspect one will drive more signups. So you run an A/B test: randomly show half your visitors CTA A, the other half CTA B, and measure which one converts better.
This seems straightforward. But underneath that simplicity lurks something messier: you’re trying to detect a tiny signal buried in pure noise.
Each visitor who lands on your page is like a weighted coin flip. Heads = they sign up. Tails = they don’t. CTA A might have a 22% chance of heads. CTA B might have an 18% chance. That 4% difference is real, but it’s small. And when you only see each visitor once, figuring out whether a 4% difference actually exists is a problem that requires tools. Statistical tools. Frequentist tools. Tools that, despite their precision, have a fundamental blind spot.
To know whether you actually detected a real difference, you need to understand what you’re actually measuring.

title: marketing analytics
text:
What You’re Estimating (And How)
Here’s the formal version of what’s happening.
Each visitor either signs up (a 1) or doesn’t (a 0). Under the hood, that’s a Bernoulli distribution — a coin flip with a bias. CTA A flips a coin biased toward signup with probability πA. CTA B flips a coin biased toward signup with probability πB.
The thing you care about is θ (theta) — the difference: θ = πA − πB.
In the real world, you don’t know πA or πB. But you can estimate them. If 220 out of 1,000 visitors who see CTA A sign up, your estimate of πA is 0.22. Same for B: 180 out of 1,000 gives you πB = 0.18. So your estimate of the difference is:
\[\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B = 0.22 - 0.18 = 0.04\]
This θ̂ (theta-hat) is your estimator. It’s a specific function of your data. And here’s the key insight: the fact that you have an estimator means you can now ask a scientific question.
Does this estimate get closer to the truth as you gather more data?

title: marketing analytics
text:
Simulating Data
Here’s where most people get confused about statistics.
In the real world, you never know the true values of πA and πB. That’s the whole problem. You run your test, you get an estimate, and you have to decide whether to trust it — all without ever knowing whether you’re right.
But we’re going to do something that sounds backwards: we’re going to pretend we know the truth. We’ll set πA and πB ourselves, generate fake visitor data under those conditions, and then ask: can our statistical tools recover the truth we planted?
It’s like a test of the tools themselves. If our estimator can’t find a true effect we put there on purpose, it’s broken. If it can, we know it’s at least doing something right.
For this exercise, let’s say: - CTA A has a true signup rate of πA = 0.22 (22%) - CTA B has a true signup rate of πB = 0.18 (18%) - So the true difference is θ = 0.04 (4 percentage points)
We’ll generate 1,000 visitors seeing CTA A and 1,000 seeing CTA B. Each visitor is a Bernoulli coin flip — heads (1) if they sign up, tails (0) if they don’t. We’ll store these simulated visitors so we can test our statistical tools on them throughout the rest of this article.

import numpy as np

# Set random seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)

# We're in a world where we know the truth
n = 1000
pi_A = 0.22  # True signup rate for CTA A
pi_B = 0.18  # True signup rate for CTA B

# Simulate 1,000 visitor outcomes for each CTA
# 1 = signup, 0 = no signup
visits_A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
visits_B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

# Quick sanity check: what did we actually observe?
print(f"Observed signup rate for A: {visits_A.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Observed signup rate for B: {visits_B.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Observed difference: {(visits_A.mean() - visits_B.mean()):.4f}")
print(f"True difference: 0.04")

Observed signup rate for A: 0.2160
Observed signup rate for B: 0.1780
Observed difference: 0.0380
True difference: 0.04


Notice: our observed rates (0.22 and 0.18) are close to but not exactly equal to the truth (0.22 and 0.18). That’s noise. That’s why we need statistics.
Now we have data. Let’s see what our tools can learn from it.

section: Does More Data Help? (The Law of Large Numbers)
text:
Does More Data Help? (The Law of Large Numbers)
The Law of Large Numbers is one of those boring-sounding theorems that changes everything.
It says: as your sample gets bigger, your sample average converges to the true population average. Imagine you’re flipping a coin repeatedly and tracking the running average of heads. With 10 flips, you might get 40% heads (fluky). With 100 flips, you get closer to 50%. With 1,000 flips, even closer. By infinity, you’d hit exactly 50%.
For your A/B test, this means something concrete: if CTA A really is 22% better than CTA B, and you keep gathering more visitors, your estimate θ̂ will eventually drift toward the true θ = 0.04 and stay there.
Here’s what that looks like in practice. Imagine you simulate this: flip 1,000 visitors for each CTA, compute the running difference after 1 visitor, after 2, after 3, all the way to 1,000. Plot it.

import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Using the simulated data from the previous section,
# compute the cumulative mean of the difference
differences = visits_A - visits_B
theta_hat = np.cumsum(differences) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

# Create interactive plot
fig = go.Figure()

# Add the running mean line
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=np.arange(1, n + 1),
    y=theta_hat,
    mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='rgb(0, 100, 200)', width=2),

              annotation_text="True θ = 0.04", annotation_position="right")

    xaxis_title="Sample Size (visitors per group)",

Figure 1: Running average of the difference (θ̂) converges to the true difference (θ = 0.04) as sample size grows. Early samples are noisy; later samples settle.




See how it bounces around wildly at first? That’s noise. Flukes. A stretch of visitors who just happened to convert more. But as you add more visitors, the bouncing stops. The line finds the truth.
The Law of Large Numbers guarantees this will happen — eventually. But “eventually” might be never in a business sense. You can’t wait for infinity. You have to make a decision with a fixed number of visitors. And here’s where convergence gets weird: knowing that θ̂ converges to θ tells you nothing about how confident you should be with a sample size of 1,000.
You need to measure how uncertain θ̂ actually is.

title: marketing analytics
section: How Uncertain Is It? (Bootstrap Standard Errors)
text:
How Uncertain Is It? (Bootstrap Standard Errors)
Uncertainty needs a number. Not a feeling. A number.
Here’s one way to think about it: if you ran this exact A/B test 1,000 times, over and over, you’d get 1,000 slightly different estimates of θ. They’d cluster around the true value, but each run would give you something different, depending on which visitors you happened to sample.
The spread of those estimates — their standard deviation — is the uncertainty. It’s called the standard error.
You could calculate the standard error using a formula. But there’s another way: the bootstrap. Resample from your observed data (with replacement) many times. Compute θ̂ for each resample. Take the standard deviation of those resampled estimates. That’s your standard error.
Here’s why this matters: you don’t need to know the mathematical formula. You just need data and computing power.

# Bootstrap standard error
n_bootstrap = 1000
theta_boots = np.zeros(n_bootstrap)

np.random.seed(42)  # For reproducibility
for i in range(n_bootstrap):
    boot_A = np.random.choice(visits_A, size=len(visits_A), replace=True)
    boot_B = np.random.choice(visits_B, size=len(visits_B), replace=True)
    theta_boots[i] = boot_A.mean() - boot_B.mean()

# Standard error from bootstrap
se_boot = np.std(theta_boots, ddof=1)
print(f"Bootstrapped SE: {se_boot:.4f}")

# Compare to analytical SE formula
p_A = visits_A.mean()
p_B = visits_B.mean()
n_A = n_B = n
se_analytical = np.sqrt((p_A * (1 - p_A) / n_A) + (p_B * (1 - p_B) / n_B))
print(f"Analytical SE: {se_analytical:.4f}")

# 95% confidence interval
ci_lower = np.percentile(theta_boots, 2.5)
ci_upper = np.percentile(theta_boots, 97.5)
print(f"95% CI: [{ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f}]")

Bootstrapped SE: 0.0175
Analytical SE: 0.0178
95% CI: [0.0040, 0.0720]


The bootstrap gives you a distribution of plausible estimates. From that distribution, you can extract a confidence interval: “the true difference is probably somewhere in this range, with 95% confidence.”
But a confidence interval is only useful if you understand its shape. And the shape is determined by something surprising.

title: marketing analytics
section: The Shape of Your Uncertainty (The Central Limit Theorem)
text:
The Shape of Your Uncertainty (The Central Limit Theorem)
Here’s where things get elegant.
No matter what distribution your data comes from — Bernoulli coin flips, in this case — the sampling distribution of your estimate becomes approximately Normal as your sample size grows. Bell curve. Symmetric. Predictable.
This is the Central Limit Theorem. It’s the theorem that made frequentist statistics possible.
Why does a Normal distribution matter so much? Because we know exactly what it looks like. We know where the tails are. We can say: “my estimate is here, and under the null hypothesis, this is how extreme that is.” That’s where p-values come from. That’s where the math becomes a decision tool.
Watch what happens as you increase sample size:

from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
n_simulations = 1000
results = {}

np.random.seed(42)
for n_size in sample_sizes:
    theta_estimates = np.zeros(n_simulations)

    for j in range(n_simulations):
        visits_A_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n_size)
        visits_B_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n_size)
        theta_estimates[j] = visits_A_sim.mean() - visits_B_sim.mean()

    results[n_size] = theta_estimates

# Create 2x2 subplot grid
fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, subplot_titles=[f"n = {n}" for n in sample_sizes])

for idx, n_size in enumerate(sample_sizes):
    row = (idx // 2) + 1
    col = (idx % 2) + 1

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Histogram(x=results[n_size], nbinsx=30,
                     marker_color='rgb(0, 100, 200)',
                     showlegend=False,
                     hovertemplate='θ̂: %{x:.3f}<br>Frequency: %{y}<extra></extra>'),
        row=row, col=col
    )

    # Update axes
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="θ̂", range=[-0.1, 0.15], row=row, col=col)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Frequency", row=row, col=col)

fig.update_layout(height=700, width=900, showlegend=False)
fig.show()



                            
                                            


Figure 2: Sampling distribution of θ̂ becomes progressively more Normal as sample size increases. At n=25, it’s bumpy. At n=500, it’s a smooth bell curve.




At n=25, the distribution is rough and asymmetric. It doesn’t look like anything special. But jump to n=500, and it’s a pristine bell curve. Almost magical.

title: marketing analytics
section: Turning Evidence into a Decision (Hypothesis Testing and Regression)
text:
Turning Evidence into a Decision (Hypothesis Testing and Regression)
Now comes the formal decision.
Your null hypothesis is: there is no difference. θ = 0. CTA A and CTA B convert at exactly the same rate.
You want to know: do your data provide enough evidence to reject this?
Here’s how frequentist hypothesis testing works. You take your estimate θ̂, divide it by its standard error, and get a z-score:
\[z = \frac{\hat{\theta} - 0}{SE(\hat{\theta})}\]
Under the null hypothesis, this z-score follows a standard Normal distribution — mean 0, standard deviation 1. So you know: if the null is true, what’s the probability of observing a z-score this extreme or more extreme?
That probability is your p-value.
Here’s the thing nobody mentions: this same test is mathematically identical to fitting a simple regression.
Stack your data into a single dataset. One column: the outcome (1 if signup, 0 if not). Another column: a treatment indicator (1 if CTA A, 0 if CTA B). Fit:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i\]
The coefficient β₁ estimates the difference in means. Its standard error, t-statistic, and p-value will match your hypothesis test (up to rounding). The machinery is identical.

from scipy import stats
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Hypothesis test approach
theta_hat = visits_A.mean() - visits_B.mean()
z_stat = (theta_hat - 0) / se_analytical
p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))
print(f"z-statistic: {z_stat:.4f}")
print(f"p-value: {p_value:.4f}\n")

# Regression approach
data = pd.DataFrame({
    'Y': np.concatenate([visits_A, visits_B]),
    'D': np.concatenate([np.ones(n), np.zeros(n)])
})

# Fit OLS regression
X = data[['D']]
y = data['Y']
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

# Get regression statistics
from scipy.stats import t as t_dist
y_pred = model.predict(X)
residuals = y - y_pred
rss = np.sum(residuals**2)
mse = rss / (len(y) - 2)
var_covar = mse * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)
se_coef = np.sqrt(np.diag(var_covar))
t_stat = model.coef_[0] / se_coef[0]
p_value_reg = 2 * (1 - t_dist.cdf(abs(t_stat), len(y) - 2))

print(f"Regression Results:")
print(f"β₁ (coefficient): {model.coef_[0]:.4f}")
print(f"SE(β₁): {se_coef[0]:.4f}")
print(f"t-statistic: {t_stat:.4f}")
print(f"p-value: {p_value_reg:.4f}")

z-statistic: 2.1388
p-value: 0.0325

Regression Results:
β₁ (coefficient): 0.0380
SE(β₁): 0.0126
t-statistic: 3.0232
p-value: 0.0025


Both approaches give the same answer because they’re asking the same question in different languages.
And the machinery works beautifully — as long as you use it the way it was designed.

title: marketing analytics
section: The Protocol Is the Test (The Problem with Peeking)
text:
The Protocol Is the Test (The Problem with Peeking)
Now your boss gets impatient.
Instead of waiting for all 1,000 visitors, she wants to check the results after every 100 visitors. If any of those early peeks shows statistical significance at α = 0.05, she declares a winner.
This is called peeking. Or sequential testing if you’re being technical. And it breaks everything.
Think of it like lottery tickets. Each peek is another chance to win the jackpot. A single ticket has a 5% chance of winning. But if you buy 10 tickets and check them one by one, your odds of winning something are much higher. Each individual check uses the same winning criteria, but the cumulative odds are different.
A single hypothesis test at α = 0.05 has a 5% false positive rate. If there’s truly no difference, you have a 5% chance of wrongly declaring one.
But when you run 10 tests on accumulating data, each peek is another chance to get a false positive. The math says the cumulative false positive rate should be roughly 1 − (0.95)^10 = 40%. In practice, it’s lower — around 20% — but still catastrophically higher than 5%.
Let’s prove this with a simulation. Assume there’s no real difference: πA = πB = 0.20. Generate 1,000 observations for each group. Then peek after every 100 visitors, testing at each checkpoint. Count how many of 10,000 simulated experiments produced at least one false positive.

np.random.seed(42)

n_experiments = 10000
n_per_peek = 100
n_peeks = 10
false_positives = 0

for exp in range(n_experiments):
    # Generate fresh data for this experiment
    # Under null hypothesis: πA = πB = 0.20 (no difference)
    visits_A_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, n_per_peek * n_peeks)
    visits_B_null = np.random.binomial(1, 0.20, n_per_peek * n_peeks)

    for peek in range(1, n_peeks + 1):
        n_current = peek * n_per_peek

        # Subset accumulated data up to this peek
        A_accum = visits_A_null[:n_current]
        B_accum = visits_B_null[:n_current]

        # Compute z-statistic on accumulated data
        p_A_null = A_accum.mean()
        p_B_null = B_accum.mean()
        se_null = np.sqrt((p_A_null * (1 - p_A_null) / n_current) +
                          (p_B_null * (1 - p_B_null) / n_current))

        if se_null > 0:
            z_null = (p_A_null - p_B_null) / se_null
            p_val = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_null)))

            if p_val < 0.05:
                false_positives += 1
                break  # Stop after first false positive in this experiment

empirical_fpr = false_positives / n_experiments
print(f"Empirical false positive rate under peeking: {empirical_fpr:.4f}")
print(f"Nominal false positive rate (single test): 0.05")
print(f"Inflation factor: {empirical_fpr / 0.05:.2f}x")

Empirical false positive rate under peeking: 0.1864
Nominal false positive rate (single test): 0.05
Inflation factor: 3.73x


The empirical false positive rate jumps from 5% to somewhere between 20% and 25%.
This is not a flaw in the test. The test is working correctly. The test is answering the question it was asked: “If I run this test right now, what’s the probability of a false positive?” Each individual test has a 5% false positive rate.
The problem is that you’re using the test as a sequential decision tool when it was designed as a point-in-time decision tool. You’re running it 10 times on the same data, each time asking “is it significant yet?” The cumulative answer to that question is totally different from the answer to “is it significant?”
This is the insight that breaks your brain. Everything was right. The formula, the calculation, the significance threshold — all correct. But the protocol — the way you decided to interact with the test — invalidated the whole thing.

title: marketing analytics
text:
The Reframe
So what does this mean for A/B testing in the real world?
It means that statistical significance is not a property of data. It’s a property of a process. The test doesn’t tell you whether your finding is true. It tells you whether your decision-making process is legitimate.
This is why the test works when followed as designed: you pre-register your sample size, you don’t peek, you run the test once, you make a decision. The protocol is honest.
But in the real world? That uplift you’ve been waiting for — the one that never came? It might not have been because the test was wrong. It might have been because someone looked at it on day three, saw a p-value of 0.048, and made a decision. Every “statistically significant” result needs an audit: When did you decide to stop? Did you peek? Did you test multiple hypotheses and report only the winning one? Did you adjust your sample size mid-experiment?
The math was never the problem. The protocol was.
Which means trusting an A/B test isn’t about understanding the formula. It’s about understanding the discipline.

title: Design & Build Decisions
text:
Append-only log of non-obvious tradeoffs. Each entry answers three questions: what was decided, why, when it might be worth revisiting.

Pre-2026-04-15 decisions (entries 1–45) live in the archive with full prose. This file indexes them as one-liners so an LLM can scan them fast and only deep-dive when needed.
New decisions (2026-04-15 onward) are written directly in this file with full prose. Append at the bottom.

When you make a non-obvious tradeoff, add an entry here before moving on. A “non-obvious tradeoff” is any choice a future reader (or future LLM) would question without the reasoning.



Full text in _archive/decisions.md.



Output directory docs/ not _site/ — GitHub Pages reads /docs on main, no gh-pages branch needed.
theme: none + minimal: true — strips Bootstrap and Quarto scaffolding; design is 100% custom.
All CSS in one file (styles/custom.css) — one place for colors, one place for components.
JS inlined via _partials/scripts.html (not <script src>) — solves relative-path problem on nested pages.
Dark mode default via inline <script> in <head> — fires before first paint, prevents flash.
Active nav link detected by JS, not hardcoded — same navbar HTML in every page.
render: ["*.qmd"] glob — excludes info.md from being rendered to HTML.
Subdirectory pages use ../ nav paths — only structural difference between root and projects/ pages.
Case studies live in projects/ subfolder — keeps root to 4 top-level pages.
No Quarto navbar (navbar: false) — custom <header> avoids Bootstrap dependency.





Light-mode overrides in a dedicated html:not(.dark) block at end of CSS — audit-friendly, no dark-mode regressions.
.t-dim (#888) and .blink-cursor global, not light-scoped — terminal is always dark, fix is unconditional.
Accent changed #2563EB → #3B82F6 — meets WCAG AA on dark background (5.1:1).





.p-card “Read more” pinned via flexbox column, not fixed height — handles variable description length.
Cell E targeted by .cell-contact class, not :has() — explicit > fragile pseudo-class support.
h1.hero-name reset block added — defeats Quarto’s injected h1 styles without !important.
Bio split into two <p> tags with inline margin-bottom — intentional rhetorical beat.
Cell D = philosophy cell with .c-quote + .c-building-sub — promotes the memorable line.
.cell-available accent top border — draws the eye to recruiter-relevant info.
Liquid glass scoped away from .terminal-cell — terminal is semantically opaque (code env, not UI panel).
Light-mode glass cells use box-shadow outline, not border — works with background-clip: padding-box.
Dark .btn-primary = glass; light = solid + shadow — asymmetric handling, glass is a dark-mode pattern.





Light-mode blob — opacity 0.28, mix-blend-mode: multiply, blur 32px — visible without palette conflict.
Cursor blob: global listener, MAX_DRIFT=120px, 3s idle reset — ambient, never freezes mid-drift.
.hero-wrap full-viewport width; constraints on .hero-inner — lets dot grid bleed edge-to-edge.
Dot grid = cursor spotlight (no lerp) + grid parallax (lerp 0.035) — two separate effects for two qualities.
Light-mode blob rewritten → monochromatic depth vignette (superseded by #27).
Light-mode blob settled on indigo at 20% — mirrors dark’s warm-cool tension on a warm canvas.
Sticky navbar fix — glass-system block was overriding position: sticky with relative.
Blob gradients: radial-gradient(circle at 50% 50%, ...) everywhere — spherical, not rectangular sweep.





projects.json = single source of truth for project cards — one file, no HTML-in-two-places duplication.
Whole card clickable via delegated click handler — guard with e.target.closest('a') to prevent double-nav.
Case study template: include-before-body for navbar only — inline {=html} for data; Pandoc $vars$ don’t work in raw includes.
Traway uses a bridge page, not a direct external link — keeps clicks inside the portfolio.
Banner-to-grid spacing: .page-banner ~ .projects-section { padding-top: 0 } — sibling selector, doesn’t touch the homepage case.
.p-desc clamp raised to 3 lines + min-height: 60px — ensures impact metric is visible; even row heights.
.p-card:focus-visible + this.blur() on click — keyboard accessibility preserved, no stuck focus ring.
Category filter bar generated from JSON — add a category = set "category": "..." in JSON, button appears.
Card borders: subtle 1px base + refined blue/violet shadow layering on hover — rejects border-image (conflicts with border-radius).
Bento cell hover: box-shadow glow layers only, no border lines — shadows don’t bleed onto neighbors.
Project card hover shadows: pronounced blue+violet layered glow — gradient effect without border-image.
Filter button borders at rgba(240,238,232,0.25) — readable at 2.5× the previous subtle border.
Badge (Open to Opportunities) gets hover scale + green glow — ties to pulsing dot’s semantics.





sync-scripts.py pre-render hook — js/main.js is SoT; _partials/scripts.html is auto-generated and gitignored.
CSS cleanup — removed old .cell duplicates and transition: all; explicit property transitions throughout.

Decision: Introduced CLAUDE.md at the repo root as the single entry point for any LLM working on the site, with supporting docs in docs-meta/ (design system, content model, build & deploy, file map, this decisions log). Originals (architecture.md, decisions.md, codex_design.md) moved to docs-meta/_archive/ via git mv to preserve history.
Why: Before this change, three sibling markdown files sat at the repo root with no index and no rule for which to load first or which to update after a change. An LLM arriving cold had to scan all three to orient, and updates drifted because nobody knew which file owned what. A single entry point + split-by-concern supporting docs means the LLM loads only what the task needs, and a “what to update when” protocol in CLAUDE.md tells it which doc to refresh. docs-meta/ (not docs/) because Quarto’s build output already owns /docs — naming collision would be a real footgun.
When to revisit: If the site grows a second audience (a human wiki, a public contributor’s guide), the CLAUDE.md + docs-meta split may no longer serve both audiences well — consider a separate README.md for humans while keeping CLAUDE.md LLM-focused.
